028998ee-babc-4096-9b28-001bc2f9a84e.summary:
Tomos Ellis, a 15-year-old male with no documented past medical history, medications, or allergies, presented to the ED on 07/01/2026 with 3 days of constant dull lower abdominal pain, constipation, reduced appetite, and mild nausea without vomiting or fever. Pain was rated 6–7/10 and worsened with eating. Examination showed mild dehydration, mild abdominal distension, lower abdominal tenderness, and mildly hypoactive bowel sounds, without guarding, rebound tenderness, or peritonism. Observations were stable.

Abdominal X-ray demonstrated significant faecal loading with no obstruction or perforation. FBC, U&Es, CRP, and LFTs were normal. He was diagnosed with constipation and mild dehydration and admitted to the paediatric ward for supportive management. Treatment included IV 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL over 4 hours, a single 10 mg dose of bisacodyl, oral macrogol/Movicol 1 sachet three times daily, oral hydration, and monitoring of bowel movements. No surgery was required.

On 07–08/01, he received advice on hydration, dietary fibre, and mobilisation. Physiotherapy sessions involved walking, stretching, and light exercises to support bowel motility; these were well tolerated, with reduced discomfort reported during movement on 08/01. Dietetic review recommended a high-fibre diet including whole grains, fruits, and vegetables. The plan on 08/01 was to continue macrogol and hydration, assess for a bowel movement, and consider discharge if symptoms improved.

On 09/01/2026, oral macrogol was discontinued. He was prescribed take-home lactulose 10 mL twice daily as required for maintenance and discharged with advice to maintain a high-fibre diet, adequate oral hydration, and ongoing light walking to help prevent recurrence.

04df53ea-55c1-48d9-84a1-1f15c133b29b.summary:
- **01/01/2026:** Allan Victor Robinson, 67-year-old man with hypertension and osteoarthritis, no known drug allergies and no regular medications documented, presented to A&E with acute confusion after a minor fall. He was triage category 2, with GCS 12/15 and disorientation to time and place; initial BP was 170/95 and pulse 88. Urgent blood tests and CT head were arranged to exclude intracranial injury. Blood samples were sent for FNC, electrolytes and coagulation studies. CT head demonstrated a **subdural hygroma**, and admission to the Neurology Ward was planned. He remained haemodynamically stable with no external injuries.
- **01/01/2026:** Physiotherapy noted mild confusion, slight gait unsteadiness and no significant falls risk; daily balance and mobility therapy was planned. Occupational therapy identified mild fine-motor difficulties affecting buttons and utensil use, with therapy planned for ADLs and adaptive strategies. His next of kin was updated.
- **02/01/2026:** Speech and language assessment showed an adequate swallow without aspiration. Communication was appropriate overall, with mild word-finding difficulty attributed in the note to residual confusion; no ongoing swallowing or speech intervention was required unless symptoms persisted.
- **04/01/2026:** Discharge planning included social work home assessment, continued daily physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and reassessment for discharge. During physiotherapy he managed five stairs with a handrail using minimal supervision and verbal cues. Mobility and balance were improving; mild residual confusion remained, although he was alert and oriented to person and place.
- **05/01/2026:** Atorvastatin 40 mg once daily was commenced as a 7-day course for cardiovascular risk. Physiotherapy assessment showed resolution of confusion, GCS 15/15, independent walking for 15 metres, steady gait, and good balance and coordination. He was cleared for independent mobility with home exercises; no further physiotherapy was required. Social work discussed discharge support and recommended community support services.
- **06/01/2026:** Education was provided regarding dizziness/confusion management, falls prevention and post-discharge safety.
- **07/01/2026:** The patient was clinically stable without residual confusion or neurological deficits. Final physiotherapy confirmed independence with walking, five stairs using a handrail and obstacle navigation; GCS was 15/15. He was considered fit for discharge with no further physiotherapy needs and was advised to continue light mobility exercises at home. Discharge planning was completed, with neurology clinic follow-up arranged.

05192757-942f-460d-b4ff-004ec39cc5ee.summary:
- **21/12/2025 – Preoperative assessment:** Hope Chinwo was evaluated for severe, gradually worsening left hip pain due to end-stage osteoarthritis, associated with stiffness and limited mobility. Medical history included hypertension, severe left hip OA, and cataract surgery in 2018. BP was 145/85 mmHg and Hb 11.3 g/dL, consistent with mild anaemia; she was taking ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily, paracetamol as needed, and calcium/vitamin D supplements. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ischaemic changes. No allergies were reported. She was deemed suitable for spinal anaesthesia, consented for elective total left hip replacement, and cleared for admission on 02/01/2026.

- **02/01/2026 – Admission and surgery:** Preoperative checks confirmed identity, fasting status, correct left hip site, medication reconciliation, and suitability to proceed. Mild anaemia had been optimised following ferrous sulfate, and elevated BP was considered consistent with known hypertension without acute concerns. She underwent spinal-anaesthetic total left hip replacement for end-stage OA. Severe degenerative changes with significant cartilage loss were found; the left femoral head was removed and a cemented prosthesis implanted. Estimated blood loss was approximately 150 mL, with no intraoperative complications. Postoperative management included enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, regular paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours, and early mobilisation with physiotherapy.

- **02/01/2026 – Immediate postoperative course:** In PACU, observations were stable (BP 130/85, HR 72, RR 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air). She was alert and oriented, with no nausea or vomiting and only mild discomfort treated with IV paracetamol. The surgical site was clean and dry, and she was transferred to the orthopaedic ward. Her GP was contacted with an update; no treatment changes were advised.

- **03/01/2026:** The plan was to encourage oral hydration and an iron-rich diet, continue daily physiotherapy and enoxaparin, and review the Hb trend. Physiotherapy focused on stair navigation; she demonstrated improved confidence and strength using a walker and handrail without pain or safety issues. Occupational therapy addressed bed transfers, dressing, hip precautions, and safe use of mobility aids. She required minimal assistance and was advised to avoid hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, internal rotation, and adduction. A raised toilet seat and bathroom grab bars were recommended, with arrangements made for delivery before discharge.

- **04/01/2026:** Physiotherapy progressed her from a walker to crutches. She demonstrated good balance and coordination while maintaining hip precautions. Nutritional review recommended a high-protein diet, including meat, fish, eggs, and legumes, with supplements if appetite remained reduced. No medication changes were made.

- **05/01/2026:** Final physiotherapy assessment found her safe to mobilise independently with crutches, including gait, transfers, turning, and navigating simulated home obstacles while maintaining hip precautions. Discharge was planned for 06/01/2026. The intended discharge plan included rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily for 7 days, ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily for postoperative anaemia, a high-iron diet, outpatient physiotherapy, and follow-up appointments. She and her daughter received postoperative care and hip-precaution instructions.

0c04d9fb-d8d0-4ee0-8fc9-0c3f7f148bdf.summary:
Georgina Claire Gurung is a woman with end-stage left hip osteoarthritis, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and mild osteopenia. Before surgery she reported four years of progressively worsening deep left hip pain, stiffness, reduced range of motion and difficulty walking, with pain up to 8/10. Pre-operative assessment on 20/12/2025 showed BP 148/92 mmHg and mild anaemia (Hb 10.8 g/dL); ECG and urinalysis were normal, with no known allergies or previous anaesthetic complications. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily for two weeks were prescribed, GP review of antihypertensive therapy was advised, and ibuprofen was to be stopped 48 hours before surgery. Consent was obtained for elective total left hip replacement under general anaesthesia with planned spinal block.

The total left hip replacement was performed electively on 03/01/2026 under general anaesthesia. Estimated blood loss was 300 mL without transfusion. Post-operatively she remained cardiovascularly and respiratorily stable with oxygen saturation 98% on room air, was drowsy but rousable without focal neurological deficits, and had no nausea, vomiting, bleeding or other documented complications. Pain was initially 4/10 and improved after IV morphine; regular paracetamol and ibuprofen were used, with tramadol prescribed as required. Enoxaparin and 24 hours of IV cefuroxime were commenced post-operatively. She was transferred to the trauma and orthopaedics ward for routine monitoring.

Physiotherapy began on 03/01/2026 with bed-edge sitting, ankle pumps, leg lifts and assisted walking using a walker; she tolerated partial weight-bearing with minimal discomfort. Subsequent sessions progressed gait, balance, transfers, stair practice and use of crutches. Occupational therapy assessed home safety and recommended a raised toilet seat, bathroom grab rails and a long-handled reacher. By 05/01 she was mobilising short distances with a walker, managing transfers, climbing simulated stairs, and performing dressing, meal preparation and other activities of daily living independently. The wound was clean with no signs of infection, pain was satisfactorily controlled with paracetamol 500 mg twice daily, and Hb remained documented at 10.8 g/dL. Ibuprofen was discontinued; dalteparin 5000 units subcutaneously was continued for thromboprophylaxis until discharge.

On 06/01/2026 she independently mobilised and navigated stairs with crutches, with minimal discomfort, and met mobility discharge criteria. She was discharged with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for two weeks, continuation of the home exercise programme, and GP follow-up in six weeks for wound review and outpatient physiotherapy referral.

0f438665-d430-4adb-8acc-c3beed9e4942.summary:
Jack Geoffrey Gray, documented as a 3-year-old male with no past medical or family history of note and allergies to pollen and macrolides, presented via A&E on 06/01/2026 with poor feeding, mild lethargy, fever, reduced urine output and nasal congestion. Initial observations were temperature 38.3°C, HR 120 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% on room air, without respiratory distress or severe dehydration. Examination showed dry mucous membranes, mildly delayed capillary refill and reduced oral intake, consistent with mild dehydration and a viral illness/viral URTI.

Paracetamol suspension 120 mg/5 mL, 5 mL, was given for fever. A 10 mL/kg normal saline bolus was administered orally and tolerated well, followed by advice for small, frequent doses of oral rehydration solution. He was accepted to the Paediatric Assessment Unit and commenced on IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose at 75% maintenance, with monitoring of fluid balance, intake/output and hydration.

During the 06/01 ward review, he remained mildly febrile and reluctant to feed, with slight improvement after IV fluids and no vomiting or diarrhoea. Observations included HR 115, BP 90/50, RR 34, temperature 37.9°C and oxygen saturation 98%. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.33 and bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, documented as mild metabolic acidosis; no other blood abnormalities were reported. Nasal congestion and mucosal swelling were present without respiratory distress.

Dietary review recommended small, frequent oral feeds, easily digestible foods, preferred fluids and regular ORS. Parents were educated regarding signs of dehydration and advised to use saline nasal drops to improve congestion and feeding. ENT review on 07/01 found moderate nasal mucosal inflammation consistent with viral URTI, without purulent discharge or anatomical abnormality. Hydration and feeding had improved, and fever had resolved.

On 07/01, parents received advice regarding continued hydration, feeding, nasal saline and recognition of deterioration. Discharge planning included PRN paracetamol, continued saline nasal drops, saline nasal spray/irrigation and advice on steam inhalation for nasal clearance.

On 08/01/2026, the patient was clinically stable, afebrile and eating and drinking better, with no hydration concerns. Parents understood the discharge advice and were confident with home care. He was discharged with continued saline nasal drops and instructions to contact GP Dr. Liu Tao if feeding or hydration worsened or other concerns arose.

136c7916-4f9b-4e5c-bf01-77e9d2c681a2.summary:
Philip Paul Cook, 49-year-old man with hypertension and mild osteoarthritis, presented on 02/01/2026 after tripping over a loose carpet edge and becoming progressively confused. He reported no loss of consciousness but felt dazed, with impaired recall of recent events. He denied headache, visual changes, nausea/vomiting, limb weakness, chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. Initial GCS was 14/15 with disorientation to time and place; pupils were equal and reactive with slightly delayed responses, and there were no focal neurological deficits or signs of head trauma. Vital signs were stable. Neurological observations were continued, and CT head imaging was expedited; the result was not documented in the provided notes.

The admission plan included IV 0.9% sodium chloride for dehydration and mild hyponatremia, neurological observations with four-hourly GCS assessments, repeat U&Es, oral hydration when appropriate, and neurology involvement. IV paracetamol 1 g four times daily was initially planned. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily was continued on 03/01/2026 as day 2 of 5. Physiotherapy addressed balance, gait stability, and mobility; he initially required moderate assistance with a Zimmer frame but showed slight improvement. Occupational therapy addressed dressing, transfers, fine motor tasks, cognitive difficulties, and adaptive equipment. A button hook, long-handled reacher, non-slip mat, and shower chair were recommended. Social work assessed home safety and discharge support.

OT documented cognitive rehabilitation for post-SDH, with mild difficulties in memory, attention, problem-solving, and planning. Speech and language assessment on 06/01/2026 found mild short-term memory and cognitive-communication difficulties, with ongoing cognitive rehabilitation recommended. He engaged with therapy and generally followed instructions, occasionally requiring verbal prompts.

Management of persistent mild hyponatremia included increased oral fluids, electrolyte-rich fluids, fluid intake adjusted to 1.5 L/day, and sodium chloride tablets 600 mg three times daily for 48 hours, with repeat U&Es planned. Discharge planning progressed with family involvement and arrangements for community physiotherapy, GP review, and home safety support.

On 08/01/2026, paracetamol 500 mg as required was planned for mild musculoskeletal discomfort. He was discharged on 09/01/2026 with stable neurological status, fall-prevention advice, and instructions to avoid anticoagulants unless prescribed. Discharge medication documentation included paracetamol 500 mg, 1–2 tablets orally four times daily as required for mild headaches for 14 days; the discharge summary also recorded paracetamol 1 g four times daily for pain. Follow-up was arranged with the neurology outpatient department in two weeks and the GP in seven days. He was advised to seek medical attention for severe headache, recurrent confusion, or other neurological symptoms.

137b8481-4f1d-4b7f-babd-20f7117023ad.summary:
- **06/01/2026:** Frank Scott Bond, with a history of hypertension, osteoarthritis and TIA (2018), presented after a minor fall with acute confusion and mild left-hip bruising. BP was 165/92 mmHg and HR 88 bpm; airway and breathing were unremarkable, with no obvious external injury. He was triaged as category 2. CT head showed a **subdural hygroma without acute intracranial haemorrhage**. He was admitted to AMU for neurological observations and conservative management, including GCS/pupil monitoring, BP monitoring, escalation if neurological deterioration occurred, and paracetamol as required for headache.  
- IV 0.9% sodium chloride was commenced for dehydration, with fluid-balance monitoring and repeat U&E testing planned. Physiotherapy and further cognitive assessment were planned if confusion persisted. Occupational therapy noted mild short-term memory and task-sequencing difficulties requiring moderate supervision, without motor deficits, and recommended cognitive rehabilitation. The next of kin was updated regarding the CT findings and management.  
- **07/01/2026:** Oral hydration with Dioralyte was continued, with repeat sodium testing and monitoring for neurological deterioration. Speech and language therapy provided cognitive training for memory, attention and problem-solving; the patient engaged well but occasionally required repetition.  
- **08/01/2026:** A family meeting addressed progress, recovery and discharge planning; a home OT assessment was planned. Speech and language assessment identified mild word-finding difficulty with complex topics, and daily cognitive-linguistic exercises were recommended.  
- **09/01/2026:** The patient showed improving cognitive clarity and resolution of headache. NaCl tablets 600 mg twice daily were continued for mild hyponatraemia. Physiotherapy addressed mobility, balance and stair climbing; strength and coordination had improved, although occasional verbal prompts were needed for safe technique. GP follow-up was discussed.  
- **10/01/2026:** IV fluids were being reduced in favour of oral hydration. Speech was clear and coherent, swallowing was normal on bedside water swallow testing, and no significant speech or swallowing deficits were present; no further SLT was required.  
- **11–12/01/2026:** Discharge arrangements and medications were completed. He was discharged home on **12/01/2026** with paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours as required for headache or joint pain, advice to maintain oral hydration, GP follow-up in two weeks, community physiotherapy referral and completed home adaptations including grab rails.

1705dd0f-011a-492c-b006-b27e03f2f4ed.summary:
- **22/12/2025 – Preoperative assessment:** Mr. Manveer Kumar, aged 87, had a 2-year history of progressively worsening right shoulder pain and stiffness, with reduced active and passive range of motion, glenohumeral tenderness, and crepitus. Diagnosis was end-stage right shoulder osteoarthritis. Medical history included hypertension, acid reflux, and bilateral cataract surgery in 2018; no known allergies were documented. Medications included paracetamol as required and omeprazole 20 mg daily.  
  Preoperative investigations showed mild anaemia (Hb 11.2 g/dL) with otherwise acceptable FBC, U&E, and LFT results; chest X-ray was normal and ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute changes. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily was started, with planned Hb monitoring. Anaesthetic assessment found him fit for general anaesthesia, with well-controlled hypertension and no identified contraindications. Consent was obtained after discussion of operative risks, benefits, recovery, and physiotherapy. Total right shoulder replacement was scheduled for 03/01/2026.

- **03/01/2026 – Surgery:** Preoperative blood tests were stable following iron treatment, with no pending results. He underwent total right shoulder replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. Severe glenohumeral cartilage loss and degeneration were found; damaged articular cartilage and subchondral bone were removed, and a cemented modular shoulder prosthesis was implanted. Blood loss was minimal and there were no complications. Postoperative management included IV cefuroxime 1.5 g every 8 hours for 24 hours, morphine PCA/IV morphine for pain, paracetamol and oral morphine as required, shoulder sling immobilisation, wound checks, and planned physiotherapy.

- **03/01/2026 – Recovery:** In recovery, he regained consciousness and responded to commands. Cardiovascular and respiratory status remained stable, with oxygen saturation 97% on room air and BP 128/76 mmHg. Mild nausea was treated with IV ondansetron. The wound had no bleeding or haematoma, and he was transferred back to Ward B3 in stable condition.

- **04/01/2026:** He remained clinically stable with normal documented observations. The right shoulder wound was clean and dry without erythema, discharge, swelling, or tenderness, and there was no evidence of compromised circulation in the right arm. Physiotherapy commenced with gentle assisted passive range-of-motion exercises, sling education, and home exercises.

- **05/01/2026:** The wound was healing well without infection or swelling, and there was no neurovascular compromise. Good passive range of motion was achieved. He reported minimal pain and improved shoulder mobility. Physiotherapy progressed to active-assisted range of motion, strengthening, sling use, self-care, and safe activities of daily living. IV paracetamol was changed to oral paracetamol 500 mg as required, with discharge planned for the following day if no new issues arose.

- **06/01/2026:** Final physiotherapy focused on active range of motion, strengthening, posture, sling use, and activities of daily living. He had no significant pain or discomfort, understood the home exercise programme, and was advised to perform it twice daily and attend follow-up physiotherapy. Orthopaedic outpatient review was planned for 6 weeks postoperatively.

1dbe23dc-0d1e-431b-81eb-497282b46a14.summary:
- **28/12/2025 – Pre-operative assessment:** Philip Clive Osborne, a 4-year-old boy, was assessed for planned removal of internal fixation from the right tibia, originally scheduled for 07/01/2026. His history included a right tibial fracture treated with internal fixation in 2024, mild asthma managed with inhalers, and eczema. Allergies included penicillin, sulfonamides, pollen, and nuts. Mild wheezing had been noted previously but there was no acute exacerbation, respiratory distress, or active infection. He was assessed as ASA II and considered fit for general anaesthesia with asthma optimisation. Montelukast 4 mg once daily was prescribed for two weeks pre-operatively, with continued salbutamol and beclometasone inhalers; two puffs of salbutamol were planned before anaesthesia. FBC and coagulation screening were performed and subsequently reviewed as satisfactory. IV cefuroxime was planned for prophylaxis, with avoidance of penicillin- and sulfonamide-based antibiotics. Informed consent was obtained from his mother after discussion of risks, benefits, recovery, pain management, and physiotherapy.
- **07/01/2026:** No new imaging was performed. Recent chest assessment and blood results were reviewed and considered acceptable for surgery. Post-operative wound care, infection monitoring, recovery expectations, and paracetamol use were discussed with his mother; paracetamol suspension was prescribed as required.
- **08/01/2026 – Procedure and recovery:** Removal of the internal fixation device from the right tibia was performed under general anaesthesia. The device was documented as removed and the surrounding tissue appeared healthy, without infection, inflammation, or other abnormality. Estimated blood loss was less than 10 mL and no complications were reported. Cefuroxime suspension was prescribed for 5 days as postoperative prophylaxis because of his penicillin and sulfonamide allergies, and paracetamol suspension was prescribed as required, with a maximum of four doses daily. A 48-hour course of IV cefuroxime was also planned, with CRP monitoring. Co-amoxiclav was additionally documented as prescribed for 5 days in the recovery documentation.
- In PACU, he remained stable on room air without respiratory or cardiovascular instability, nausea, agitation, or wound bleeding. He received one dose of oral ibuprofen 100 mg with effective pain control and was transferred to the Children’s Orthopaedic Ward. The dressing remained intact. Parents were advised to keep it clean and dry and monitor for redness, swelling, discharge, or other signs of infection.
- **08–09/01/2026 – Rehabilitation:** Physiotherapy introduced gentle ankle and knee range-of-motion exercises, weight-bearing, and supervised walking using a child-sized frame, followed by paediatric crutch training. He was cooperative and had minimal discomfort. By 09/01/2026 he mobilised independently along the ward corridor with his usual gait, without limp or pain, and performed stretches and strengthening exercises with minimal assistance. No further inpatient physiotherapy was required; parents were advised to encourage daily walking and prescribed exercises.
- **09/01/2026 – Discharge planning:** The surgical site was clean and healing well, with no signs of infection. He was alert, comfortable, and reported no pain or discomfort, with pain controlled using paracetamol. Discharge later that day was planned, with ibuprofen 100 mg liquid three times daily prescribed for additional pain relief. Follow-up was arranged for surgical review and suture removal, and the GP was informed of the procedure, postoperative plan, and need to monitor for infection or complications.

28570119-9cdc-4120-98c0-4edb76cf36a3.summary:
On 07/01/2026, Judith Ada Wells, a 39-year-old woman with no documented past medical history or allergies, presented with an exertion-associated severe headache rated 8/10. Initial BP was 160/90 mmHg and HR 88 bpm. Neurological examination was normal, with no focal deficits, altered consciousness, seizures, neck stiffness, or visual symptoms. CT head showed no intracranial haemorrhage, mass lesion, or other abnormality. Blood tests showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 ×10⁹/L), CRP 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function. RCVS was diagnosed clinically, and she was admitted under Neurology.

On 07/01/2026, nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours was started, with MRI/MRA planned. At ward review, headache persisted at 7/10 and BP was 150/92 mmHg, without new symptoms.

On 08/01/2026, MRI/MRA confirmed RCVS. Examination remained neurologically normal. CRP was 12 mg/L, the FBC and renal panel were otherwise unremarkable, and mild hypokalaemia was documented (K⁺ 3.3 mmol/L). BP had improved to 135/85 mmHg.

On 09/01/2026, physiotherapy assessment found mild residual neck stiffness without significant functional impairment. No inpatient physiotherapy was required; outpatient physiotherapy was planned after discharge.

On 10/01/2026, the plan was to repeat MRA on 11/01/2026, continue nimodipine at 30 mg every 4 hours, and use dietary measures to increase oral sodium intake and restrict excessive fluids for documented mild hyponatraemia.

On 11/01/2026, headache had improved to 2/10 with no new neurological symptoms. Repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, and discharge planning was initiated. Outpatient neurology follow-up was planned for four weeks after discharge.

On 12/01/2026, she was deemed fit for discharge. The discharge plan documented nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily, to be tapered over two weeks, neurology follow-up in four weeks, avoidance of triggers such as intense physical exertion and stress, and education about recurrence symptoms. Resolution of vasoconstriction on 11/01/2026 was documented. A subsequent GP handover recorded the discharge medication as amlodipine 5 mg once daily.

29ea304f-821d-474e-81a1-394ca3945e02.summary:
Ren Suzuki, a 40-year-old man with asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, presented to the ED on 05/01/2026 at approximately 01:00 with sudden, constant, sharp central chest pain radiating to the back, rated 8/10 and worsened by deep inspiration and movement, with mild shortness of breath. Initial observations showed sinus tachycardia (HR 110 bpm), RR 24/min, BP 135/85 mmHg, SpO₂ 96% on room air, and temperature 37.1°C. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes. Chest X-ray showed subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum, leading to a diagnosis of spontaneous pneumomediastinum.

Management was conservative, with paracetamol 1 g four times daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, avoidance of straining/heavy lifting, and monitoring for respiratory compromise. A repeat chest X-ray was planned. Omeprazole 20 mg daily was continued for gastrointestinal protection.

On 06/01, repeat chest X-ray showed slight reduction in the pneumomediastinum compared with initial imaging, and conservative management continued without medication changes. By 07/01, the patient was pain-free, so regular paracetamol and ibuprofen were stopped; repeat imaging in 48 hours was planned. On 07/01, he received education regarding recurrence symptoms and when to seek urgent medical attention.

Discharge planning began on 08/01, with no new medications or treatment changes, routine respiratory clinic follow-up arranged, and advice to monitor for recurrence. The GP was updated regarding his progress and stability. Final chest X-ray review on 09/01 showed complete resolution of the pneumomediastinum, with no subcutaneous emphysema or other abnormality; no further imaging was required, and he was cleared for discharge the following day.

31f9612b-5a6b-48ea-887b-895772a83b99.summary:
- **15/12/2025:** Evaluated for a 4-year history of progressive right knee pain due to end-stage osteoarthritis, worsening over the preceding 6 months. Pain was aching and stiff, with intermittent swelling and occasional night pain, aggravated by weight-bearing, standing, and walking. Past history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and appendectomy in 1998. ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute abnormalities; pre-operative blood results were pending.

- **18/12/2025:** Anaesthetic assessment found clear lungs, Mallampati II airway, and BP 148/92 mmHg, considered acceptable for surgery. The patient was assessed as fit for general anaesthesia. Amlodipine 5 mg daily had recently been started for blood-pressure optimisation. Ibuprofen was to be stopped one week before surgery, with paracetamol 1 g four times daily prescribed instead. Oral midazolam 2 mg was planned on the morning of surgery for anxiety.

- **20/12/2025:** Informed consent was obtained for elective total right knee replacement, including discussion of benefits, infection, DVT, stiffness, anaesthetic complications, pain management, and recovery. No known drug allergies were documented.

- **01/01/2026:** Pre-operative ECG and blood tests were reviewed and were acceptable for surgery. The patient underwent total right knee replacement under general anaesthesia for end-stage right knee osteoarthritis. Operative findings included significant cartilage erosion and osteophyte formation. Severely eroded cartilage and osteophytes were removed, and a cemented total knee prosthesis was implanted. Blood loss was minimal and no complications were reported. Post-operative morphine PCA and cefuroxime 1.5 g IV for 24 hours were commenced.

- **01/01/2026 postoperative:** In PACU, vital signs were stable. Pain of 5/10 improved after morphine 2 mg IV. Mild nausea responded to ondansetron 4 mg IV. The patient was awake and alert and transferred to the Trauma and Orthopaedics Ward. Paracetamol 1 g four times daily and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily were prescribed. Later review documented pain of 6/10, no nausea, no signs of DVT, and a post-operative haemoglobin of 110 g/L; transfusion was not required. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily was prescribed for thromboprophylaxis.

- **02/01/2026:** Physiotherapy commenced with knee range-of-motion exercises, ankle pumps, strengthening, and partial weight-bearing with a walker. Swelling was noted as an expected post-operative change, without severe pain or increased symptoms. The plan was for daily physiotherapy and dalteparin 500 units subcutaneously daily for thromboprophylaxis until discharge. Written and verbal advice was provided regarding wound care, analgesia, mobility exercises, and signs of complications.

- **03/01/2026:** The patient achieved 90° knee flexion with assisted exercises and mobilised confidently using a walker. Mild swelling and bruising at the surgical site were considered consistent with post-operative changes. CRP was 45 mg/L, described as consistent with post-surgical inflammation. Knee mobility improved, with mild discomfort controlled on current analgesia. Ibuprofen was reduced to 200 mg three times daily, with continued daily physiotherapy and increased focus on weight-bearing exercises.

- **04/01/2026:** Final physiotherapy session focused on transitioning from a walker to crutches, stair practice, balance exercises, and the home exercise programme. The patient demonstrated safe stair climbing and obstacle navigation under supervision. Knee flexion and mobility had improved, although mild stiffness persisted. The patient was considered safe regarding physiotherapy goals and advised to continue the home exercise programme.

359014a1-10e6-4bd8-9ba7-513d021c971e.summary:
- **07/01/2026:** Bin Pan, 34-year-old man with no documented past medical history, allergies, or regular medications, presented to A&E with sudden severe sharp central chest pain radiating, without trauma. He was triage category 2. Initial assessments showed a patent airway, mild tachypnoea/accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, stable cardiovascular observations, and GCS 15. Spontaneous pneumomediastinum was suspected/diagnosed. At 01:00, tachypnoea and mild palpable subcutaneous emphysema were noted; HR was 92 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg. GCS was documented as 5/15 at that review.
- **07/01/2026:** Chest X-ray was requested to assess mediastinal air and exclude major abnormalities. He was admitted to the Acute Respiratory Ward for conservative management, analgesia, monitoring for worsening subcutaneous emphysema, respiratory distress, or haemodynamic instability, and serial chest X-rays. Paracetamol 1 g four times daily and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily were prescribed; omeprazole 20 mg daily and supportive care were also documented.
- **07/01/2026:** Social history documented that he lived alone, was independent, worked as an IT consultant, did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use recreational drugs, and cycled regularly. He appeared anxious during review.
- **08/01/2026:** Repeat chest X-ray was planned to assess resolution. He continued supportive care, mobilisation, and pain management. 8448b3fa-1f5e-45b5-bda5-eb0b7921b8cc.summary:
23-year-old woman, Dia Reddy, with no documented past medical history, presented to A&E on 04/01/2026 with severe headache, nausea, and photophobia. She was alert with GCS 15, initially haemodynamically stable, but subsequently developed fever (38.9°C), tachycardia (118 bpm), worsening headache, and mild neck stiffness. No rash or focal neurological deficits were noted. She was triaged Category 2 and admitted to the Neurology Ward under Dr Afua Asare for suspected bacterial meningitis.

Urgent blood tests showed WCC 16.5 ×10⁹/L and CRP 112 mg/L, with normal U&Es; blood cultures were sent. CT head performed at 08:15 showed no abnormality. Lumbar puncture at 08:45 demonstrated neutrophil-predominant CSF pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein. Reported CSF values included WCC 450/µL with glucose 1.5 mmol/L and protein 1.2 g/L, and later WCC 1,200/µL with glucose 1.2 mmol/L (serum glucose 5.4 mmol/L) and protein 1.8 g/L. CSF Gram stain and cultures, and blood cultures, were sent for analysis.

Treatment was initiated with IV ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily and vancomycin, with IV fluids and antiemetics as required. IV dexamethasone 10 mg four times daily was added on 05/01/2026. Repeat blood cultures and serial blood monitoring were planned, with antibiotic adjustment to be guided by CSF culture results.

By 09/01/2026, she was clinically well and stable: HR 74, BP 118/76, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on air. CSF findings were reported as improving, with reduced WCC and normalising protein, and there were no meningeal signs, focal neurological deficits, or other signs of infection.

On 09–10/01/2026, she received counselling regarding relapse symptoms and adherence to oral antibiotics. The documented oral antibiotic plans included amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily and cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily; education specified amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days. Discharge was planned for 11/01/2026 if stability continued, with neurology outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks. A printed discharge summary was provided on 11/01/2026 detailing bacterial meningitis, treatment, oral amoxicillin for 7 days, and follow-up arrangements.

900efb9a-fb57-4f25-b2a3-0a8c6f55b2d6.summary:

94264e23-ea67-496e-b027-5dd0cc334f1e.summary:
15-year-old male with asthma, seasonal allergies, and sulfonamide allergy presented to the ED on 03/01/2026 with a 3-day history of worsening wheeze, shortness of breath, cough, and chest tightness following a cold with nasal congestion and sore throat. He had no fever, chest pain, haemoptysis, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Initial observations showed tachypnoea (RR 28), audible wheeze, and SpO₂ 92% on room air.

On assessment, he was alert but in respiratory distress with bilateral expiratory wheeze, reduced air entry, accessory muscle use, and peak flow 180 L/min. SpO₂ was 91% on room air and later 93% on 2 L oxygen via nasal cannula. He received nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and ipratropium 500 micrograms at 09:25, followed by oral prednisolone 40 mg. He was admitted to the paediatric respiratory ward for an acute asthma exacerbation.

On 03/01, treatment was changed to IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly, with salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers every four hours and supplemental oxygen targeting SpO₂ above 94%. ABG showed mild respiratory acidosis (pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 6.0 kPa). Chest radiograph showed no pneumothorax or consolidation, and no infection markers were raised. Repeat blood gas monitoring and escalation to PICU if respiratory status worsened were planned.

On 04/01, he remained alert with mild respiratory distress, respiratory rate 24, and scattered expiratory wheeze; repeat blood gas was pending. On 05/01, IV hydrocortisone was discontinued and oral prednisolone 20 mg daily for three days was commenced as a reducing course. Salbutamol via spacer was increased to every two hours as needed.

By 06/01, he reported no further shortness of breath or chest tightness overnight and felt well overall.

96766f3f-aa50-4bcb-abbf-884328049ea9.summary:
16-year-old male, Minato Yoshida, presented on 05/01/2026 with a 2–3 day history of gradual-onset, persistent dull bilateral/frontal headache rated 6/10, worsened by prolonged screen use, studying, and sitting, with mild neck and shoulder tightness. He denied nausea, vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, phonophobia, neurological symptoms, fever, or neck stiffness. He had no past medical history, allergies, regular medications, or relevant family history.

Vital signs remained normal. Examination showed an alert, well-appearing patient with GCS 15, intact cranial nerves, normal strength, sensation, reflexes and gait, and no focal neurological deficits or papilloedema. Mild trapezius/neck and shoulder muscle tension was noted. CT head was normal with no acute intracranial pathology. FBC, U&E, CRP, and LFTs were normal. The working diagnosis was tension headache.

He was admitted under general medicine for observation and treated with PRN paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, with advice on hydration, regular study breaks, posture, and physiotherapy for muscle tension. Overnight he remained clinically stable, with reduced neck tension and no neurological deficits. On 06/01/2026, ibuprofen 200 mg three times daily was prescribed for residual discomfort, and he was discharged home with outpatient physiotherapy follow-up.

A 30-minute physiotherapy session on 06/01/2026 focused on neck and shoulder mobility, stretching, and posture correction. He reported markedly improved neck mobility and significantly reduced headache intensity. He was advised to continue the exercises at home, use paracetamol or ibuprofen as needed, maintain good posture and hydration, and seek medical attention if symptoms worsened or recurred.

973ee9d2-7c23-4e1d-afb2-86f679b55964.summary:
George Alfred Rehman, a 13-year-old male with no documented past medical history, presented on 05/01/2026 with a two-day history of gradual-onset constant lower abdominal pain, bloating, reduced appetite, and suspected constipation. Initial observations were within normal limits. Examination showed mild abdominal distension and tenderness. Blood tests (FBC, U&E, CRP) and an abdominal X-ray were performed. The X-ray demonstrated significant faecal loading without bowel obstruction. A 10 mg oral dose of senna was administered, and he was admitted to the paediatric ward for constipation management.

Initial treatment included macrogol one sachet three times daily, lactulose 10 mL twice daily, increased oral fluids, and monitoring of bowel movements. On 06/01, he had mild residual abdominal discomfort, was clinically stable, and had a mildly elevated CRP of 12 mg/L without systemic complications. Dietetic advice included a high-fibre diet and increased fluids. Occupational/physical therapy provided education on physical activity, abdominal massage, and exercises including seated twists and knee-to-chest stretches for home use.

By 07/01, abdominal discomfort had significantly improved, with two bowel movements overnight. He tolerated oral intake and maintained hydration. Examination showed a well-appearing, hydrated patient with a soft, non-tender, non-distended abdomen and no guarding. FBC, U&E, and CRP were documented as within normal ranges, with stable observations.

He was discharged on 07/01/2026 with lactulose 10 mL twice daily for seven days, macrogol one sachet daily for ongoing stool softening, and senna 7.5 mg nightly for five days under parental supervision. Advice included adequate hydration, a high-fibre diet, and continuation of abdominal massage and mobility exercises. Follow-up in the outpatient paediatric clinic was planned for two weeks, and the GP was informed of the discharge plan and ongoing laxative and dietary management.

9d8fd25d-c4fe-4343-8ff5-5da5dad4e740.summary:
Brian William Morris is a 76-year-old man with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, osteoarthritis and previous cataract surgery (2018), with a documented nut allergy. Pre-operative assessment on 23/12/2025 was for elective total right shoulder replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. FBC, renal function and chest X-ray were normal; ECG showed minor age-related changes without acute abnormality. Hb was 11.2 g/dL, and ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily was advised. General anaesthesia was planned, with enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily intended from admission for thromboprophylaxis. Written consent was obtained after discussion of risks and benefits, and ibuprofen was to be stopped from 30/12/2025.

On 05/01/2026, pre-operative assessment showed normal FBC, U&E and coagulation results, stable observations, and no evidence of infection or acute right shoulder deterioration. Pre-operative physiotherapy provided education on sling use, early mobilisation, pendulum exercises, and management of pain and swelling.

On 06/01/2026, he underwent total right shoulder replacement. In PACU he was haemodynamically stable with a clean, dry dressing, intact neurological status and pain rated 4/10. Mild nausea resolved after IV ondansetron; IV paracetamol was given for analgesia. Planned medications included PRN co-codamol and ondansetron. Post-operative physiotherapy commenced with gentle passive-assisted movements and education regarding posture and sling use. Wound-care education was provided.

On 07–08/01/2026, physiotherapy progressed to active-assisted range-of-motion exercises, including pendulums, assisted arm lifts, external rotation and wall climbs. He tolerated therapy without significant pain or complications and was advised to continue exercises three times daily and avoid heavy lifting with the right arm for six weeks. Elevated inflammatory markers were documented on 08/01/2026 (CRP 65 mg/L, WBC 11.5 ×10⁹/L), prompting a five-day course of oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily as prophylaxis for suspected early post-operative infection, with repeat inflammatory markers planned. Occupational therapy assessed the home environment and recommended a raised toilet seat and bathroom grab bars. Mild exercise discomfort was considered manageable with paracetamol and ibuprofen at that time.

On 09/01/2026, discharge planning included a seven-day course of co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg three times daily, co-codamol 30/500 mg for pain, dalteparin 5,000 units subcutaneously once daily for seven days for thromboprophylaxis, and discontinuation of ibuprofen due to gastrointestinal irritation risk. Final physiotherapy review confirmed independent performance of pendulum, passive arm-raise and isometric exercises with correct technique. He was discharged with a home exercise programme three times daily, sling guidance, wound-care advice, and instructions to use paracetamol or co-codamol as required and continue omeprazole. Follow-up physiotherapy was scheduled for 16/01/2026, with outpatient follow-up also documented at two weeks and six weeks post-discharge.

a8629d2e-7fd8-449a-9149-e0f5045a04c4.summary:

He was confirmed fit for the procedure, instructed to remain nil by mouth from midnight, and continued on oral ferrous sulfate. Pre-admission blood results were reviewed; no new investigations were required.

Ponseti casting was performed for congenital left clubfoot. Foot alignment was corrected as expected; there was no tissue removal, blood loss, implant, or documented complication. a9827c1c-fb54-4e5b-8bc6-d3099869e671.summary:
Jane Jill Osborne, 74, presented on 01/01/2026 with progressive breathlessness and visible shortness of breath. She required oxygen via nasal cannula, initially at 4 L/min and subsequently planned at 2 L/min. Her history included hypertension, osteoarthritis, and mild CKD stage 2; no pre-admission medications were reported. She was diagnosed with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and admitted to the Respiratory HDU under Dr Pamela Simmons. The initial plan included therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban 5 mg twice daily, low-flow oxygen, urgent CTPA to confirm CTEPH, echocardiography to assess right ventricular function, and close monitoring. Results of the requested imaging were not documented.

From 02/01, physiotherapy included seated and breathing exercises, followed by graded walking and a 6-minute walk test on 05/01. She had mild exertional dyspnoea without significant desaturation; oxygen saturation remained 93–95% on 2 L/min during the 05/01 session. Dietetic review for fatigue and mild weight loss led to advice for a high-calorie, high-protein diet. Occupational therapy identified mild fatigue during activities of daily living and provided energy-conservation advice, with recommendation for adaptive equipment. Psychological support addressed anxiety and adjustment to the CTEPH diagnosis, with outpatient support recommended.

On 04/01, cardiology assessed her for pulmonary endarterectomy and referred her to a regional PEA centre for multidisciplinary assessment; no immediate management changes were made. On 05/01, her GP was updated and asked to arrange post-discharge anticoagulation monitoring. An MDT reviewed discharge planning, oxygen needs, anticoagulation, physiotherapy, and pulmonary hypertension follow-up. By 06/01, breathing technique had improved and she felt more confident managing symptoms; home exercises and community support were arranged.

Anticoagulation plans varied during the admission. On 07/01, documentation described education regarding warfarin with enoxaparin 40 mg once daily bridging until the INR was therapeutic, with an INR check arranged through the GP in three days. The discharge plan on 08/01 documented rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily, while also documenting initiation of warfarin 5 mg once daily with LMWH bridging. Discharge education specified rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days followed by 20 mg once daily. No bleeding or adverse effects were reported in the 07/01 plan.

She was discharged home on 08/01/2026 with written instructions, anticoagulation advice and emergency pulmonary hypertension team contact details. Follow-up at the pulmonary hypertension clinic was arranged for two weeks later. Paracetamol 1 g four times daily as required was prescribed for musculoskeletal discomfort.

b70c7ff6-c2af-4df6-bd88-889bf767a168.summary:

Vital signs were normal, and the wound was clean and dry without erythema or discharge. - **10/01/2026 – Discharge:** Hb remained stable at 10.5 g/dL. The right hip wound was healing without erythema, swelling, or discharge, and observations remained stable. b8085350-6748-47a5-a12f-6acd07c40a82.summary:

The plan was to proceed with Pavlik harness application on 03/01/2026 using oral midazolam 0.5 mg/kg, with continued access to barrier cream and monitoring for skin irritation or pressure sores.

Both hips were positioned to achieve optimal reduction, with satisfactory harness positioning and no abnormalities, blood loss, or complications. Mild pre-existing nappy-area erythema did not worsen. Post-procedure observations showed stable cardiovascular and respiratory status, oxygen saturation above 98% on room air, no desaturation or bradycardia, and no distress. The patient was awake, feeding well, and settled. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 6 hours as required was prescribed.

- **03/01/2026 – Post-procedure care and therapy:** Harness fit and position remained satisfactory, with no skin irritation or pressure sores. Parents reported no concerns and the patient was feeding well. Parents received education on safe handling, lifting, positioning, dressing, nappy changes, harness care, and daily skin checks. They were advised not to adjust the straps at home and to contact the paediatric orthopaedic team for skin concerns, discomfort, or distress.
